items.abstract:
<jats:p>In streaming multimodal monitoring, modality degradations (e.g.,
sensor noise or missing data) often trigger false alarms in anomaly detectors, violating
operational constraints on the False Alarm Rate (FAR). This paper formulates the
problem of FAR-budgeted anomaly detection and proposes a Reliability-Constrained
Anomaly Detection (RC-AD) method. RC-AD utilizes online modality reliability
estimates to gate the contribution of degraded channels to the anomaly score and to
dynamically adjust thresholding logic. Evaluation on controlled streams and real air
quality data demonstrates that RC-AD maintains the FAR budget while achieving
significantly higher recall on degraded segments compared to naive multimodal
baselines.</jats:p>
title: RELIABILITY-AWARE ANOMALY DETECTION FOR STREAMING MULTIMODAL TIME SERIES IN DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate diagnosis of heart diseases relies on determining any discrepancies in time-series data of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Though Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) deliver powerful probabilistic modeling tools for anomaly detection, their accuracy drops significantly when compared to deterministic models on clean, highly aligned datasets, which is caused by posterior collapse. This paper explores and theorizes the practical limits of posterior collapse and the effectiveness of Autoencoders against a Micro-β VAE architecture (β ∈ {0.001,0.1}) combined with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) annealing schedule over ECG signals. By integrating a feature-level attention mechanism, we improve clinical interpretability. Our approach improves on the currently available deterministic Autoencoders and achieves a mean F1-score of 0.9735 when it is evaluated over five independent initializations on the ECG5000 dataset. This demonstrates increased robustness to increasing synthetic Gaussian noise. Anomalous time steps are localized by attention weights despite the stochastic nature of the latent space.</jats:p>
title: Interpretable Time-Series Anomaly Detection using Micro-β VAEs
Conditional Multimodal Fusion for Time-Series Anomaly Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) aims to identify temporally localized deviations from expected patterns in sequential data and is a fundamental task in monitoring and diagnosis. Recent TSAD methods increasingly use learned temporal representations and external pre-training, raising the question of whether comparable performance can be achieved with simpler target-series-only methods. We introduce Fusion of Representation-based Outlier Scores for Time Series (\ours{}), a lightweight ensemble for univariate time-series anomaly detection. \ours{} combines multiscale Mahalanobis distance and Isolation Forest on statistical features with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on raw windows, and averages the two largest processed component scores at each time point. On the 350-series Time-Series Benchmark for Anomaly Detection--Univariate (TSB-AD-U) evaluation split, unsupervised and semi-supervised \ours{} achieve mean Volume Under the Surface for Precision--Recall (VUS-PR) scores of 0.6320 and 0.6481, respectively, exceeding all evaluated baselines, including externally pre-trained methods. Source-level paired tests show statistically significant improvements over most baselines. On a 92-series monitoring subset, \ours{} retains sub-second median per-series processing time while achieving higher VUS-PR than every baseline with local runtime measurements. These results show that a lightweight detector ensemble can jointly deliver strong detection performance and low computational cost without external pre-training.</jats:p>
title: A Lightweight Detector Ensemble for Univariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multimodal time-series anomaly detection incorporates textual data regarding external events to provide contextual information for numerical fluctuations; this facilitates the interpretation of sudden fluctuations in complex systems—such as those caused by disasters, public events, or environmental changes—and enables the identification of numerical fluctuations that cannot be explained by the available context. However, existing methods typically treat text as an auxiliary feature for enhancement while still relying primarily on the degree of deviation in numerical sequences to detect anomalies; consequently, they struggle to distinguish between explainable fluctuations driven by genuine external events and fluctuations that are unsupported by the available event semantics. Moreover, redundant, mismatched, or weakly correlated text can disrupt the modeling of normal temporal patterns, potentially triggering cross-modal negative transfer. To address these issues, we propose SISAD, a multimodal time-series anomaly-detection method based on semantic interference suppression. First, the method employs trend decoupling and multiscale encoding to extract local temporal variation patterns, thereby mitigating the impact of low-frequency trends on the modeling of localized or fine-grained temporal variations. Second, it constructs a prototype-based semantic fusion module that integrates external event text, endogenous statistical text, and domain prior knowledge, enhancing the semantic interpretability of the current segment by retrieving learned historical prototypes. Finally, a semantic interference suppression module is designed to measure the degree of cross-modal conflict and adaptively adjust the text fusion intensity; this allows relevant text to contribute to reconstruction and discrimination while attenuating interference from unreliable text. Experiments conducted on seven datasets spanning three domains demonstrate that SISAD outperforms existing methods across most datasets and key metrics, showing improved performance in distinguishing fluctuations with relevant contextual support from those that cannot be explained by the available context. Ablation and text-perturbation experiments further support the contributions of prototype-based semantic fusion and semantic interference suppression with the evaluated settings.</jats:p>
title: SISAD: Semantic Interference Suppression for Multimodal Time-Series Anomaly Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multivariate sensor monitoring requires detecting abnormal values as well as changes in dependencies among channels. Many anomaly detectors emphasize reconstruction or forecasting residuals, or rely on a fixed sensor graph, which can miss relation anomalies and confuse benign regime changes with faults. We propose DCG-SSL, a dynamic directed-graph self-supervised framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection. For each sliding window, the method estimates a sparse lag-aware directed dependency graph from predictive evidence, matches the graph to a bank of normal relation prototypes, and fuses temporal and graph representations. Self-supervised pretraining combines masked reconstruction, future prediction, sensor-order perturbation, and relation-consistency learning with relation interventions. At inference, a validation-calibrated score decomposes anomaly evidence into node reconstruction, relation deviation, and future-prediction components. The lag-aware predictive feature is causal-inspired in a limited Granger-style sense and is not claimed to identify structural causality. Experiments on SWaT, WADI, SMD, MSL, and SMAP yield an average F1 score of 91.1%, compared with 89.0% for the strongest baseline under the same protocol. Ablation and robustness analyses associate the reported gains with dynamic directionality, normal relation prototypes, and relation-aware self-supervision. These results support dynamic relation modeling as a practical computational approach for anomaly detection in heterogeneous sensor systems.</jats:p>
title: Dynamic Directed-Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Multivariate Sensor Time-Series Anomaly Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Despite the promising performance achieved by reconstruction-based methods in recent years, these methods still struggle to effectively balance the reconstruction of normal and anomalous patterns. In contrast, contrastive learning focuses on learning relationships among time-series samples by pulling similar samples closer while pushing dissimilar samples apart. However, constructing negative samples often introduces substantial computational and memory overhead. Recent studies have explored negative-free training paradigms to alleviate this issue. Motivated by these advances, we propose \textbf{Negative-Free Contrastive Learning for Time Series Anomaly Detection (NFCL)}. For the backbone network, we employ a lightweight and efficient variant of KAN-AD to achieve a favorable balance between computational efficiency and detection performance. During training, we adopt a stop-gradient mechanism to enable negative-free contrastive learning and introduce a threshold-based early-stopping criterion. The proposed threshold-based early-stopping strategy substantially reduces training time while maintaining detection performance. Extensive experiments on the multivariate datasets of the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that NFCL achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods in both point-based and range-based anomaly detection. Furthermore, we find that incorporating a channel-dependent  mechanism into the backbone substantially improves detection performance on highly challenging datasets. In particular, NFCL achieves a 263\% improvement in VUS-PR over the previous best-performing method on this dataset.</jats:p>
title: Negative-Free Contrastive Learning for Time Series Anomaly Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>​Time series anomaly detection is critical for industrial system reliability and security. Existing methods typically operate at a single prediction scale, missing anomalies that manifest across different time horizons. We propose a Transformer-based framework combining temporally aligned multi-scale prediction, cross-scale consistency, and a variance-calibrated fusion rule with no learned parameters or per-dataset tuning of 𝛼. All horizons (1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 steps) forecast the same current state from causal contexts ending at the corresponding lags; a consistency signal measures disagreement among the same-target forecasts and flags anomalies that break cross-scale agreement. On 28 SMD server machines, under an identical EMA post-processing applied to every method, our method attains an average AUROC of 0.878, comparable to the best classical baseline (0.883), and the numerically highest AUPRC (0.494). On the HAI 21.03 industrial control system dataset, under a uniform causal evidence aggregation applied to every method, it attains the highest point-wise AUROC, F1, AUPRC, and range-based VUS-PR (0.857, 0.656, 0.504, and 0.591, with F1 at the exact oracle-optimal threshold). The same architecture template and all non-dimensional model and training hyperparameters are used across both domains, with each domain trained separately; only the causal score-aggregation rule is adapted to each dataset’s temporal characteristics. Batched GPU inference scores test windows in parallel without changing the computed anomaly scores. Case studies suggest that multi-scale prediction captures sudden failures (short horizons) and gradual drifts (long horizons),and that cross-scale consistency contributes a consistent improvement on both datasets.​​</jats:p>
title: Multi-Scale Transformer for Time Series Anomaly Detection Across Server and Industrial Control Domains ​
